items.content:
RT @VitalikButerin: I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

items.content:
This is an image we keep using in our training, because you don't want to be the man at the bottom.

In our experience, most people stop at roughly the same point: when it gets hard, they've run out of ideas, and they feel like they’ve tried everything.

When you reach that point, go for a walk, take a break, or take a shower. Give yourself some time away from the problem, then come back and push a little further.

Revisit an assumption, investigate the behaviour you couldn't quite explain, or try the idea you dismissed earlier. Coming back with a fresh perspective can help you see something you missed after hours of staring at the same code or requests.

We've seen it again and again: some of the best bugs are discovered when you push a little further after you thought you were completely done.

@Grimdoomer's I Code 4 Coffee is an incredible FREE archive of low-level game console and hardware research.

- Xbox / Xbox 360 security
- Original Xbox hardware hacking
- Halo 2 engine + OS patching
- DirectX + rendering internals
- Raspberry Pi + EEPROM hacking

AlertZero, the agentic layer of Elastic Security, is heading to technical preview.

Full walkthrough from @jamesspi, including the ES|QL query Detection Watch uses to rank rules by false-positive closures: https://t.co/9E1npJJDzn

AlertZero has 4 Watches, each a group of named agents with one SOC responsibility.

• Triage Watch: alert analysis plus Attack Discovery, one Investigation per attack
• Hunt Watch: threat research tested against your telemetry, exact lookups first, behavior second
• Detection Watch: investigates rule gaps and FPs, proposing the edit with a backtest
• Forensics Watch: reconstructs the endpoint, then proposes response actions through Elastic Defend

Every consequential change arrives as a Proposed Action. Approved and executed are logged as separate states.

items.content:
Defender kept saying the machine was clean.

But something about the laptop still did not look right.

There was a process making outbound connections in the background, and the user could not explain where it came from.

So I checked Microsoft Defender’s exclusions.

That was where I found:

C:\ProgramData\MediaCache

That folder had been excluded from Defender scanning.

Now that was a serious red flag.

I checked the Defender Operational log and found Event ID 5007 showing that the exclusion had been added the previous evening around 7:42 PM.

Then I checked the folder itself.

Less than a minute after the exclusion was created, a file called:

MediaSync.exe

appeared inside it.

The name looked normal enough, but the file was not digitally signed.

I checked the process list and confirmed the same executable was currently running in the background.

Then I checked its network activity.

It had an active HTTPS connection to an external IP address.

At that point, the timeline was becoming very clear.

First, the Defender exclusion was created.

Then the executable was dropped into that exact folder.

Then the process started running from a location Defender had been told not to scan.

So when somebody checked the machine and Defender said everything was fine, that did not necessarily mean the machine was fine.

Part of the machine had basically been removed from Defender’s normal visibility.

We isolated the laptop, collected the executable and Defender logs, preserved the exclusion configuration and started checking how that setting was added in the first place.

One thing this incident reminded me of is that security tools are only as useful as their configuration.

If malware can get its own folder excluded, you can scan the machine ten times and still feel confident for the wrong reason.

So when Defender says a suspicious machine is clean, I also like checking:

Get-MpPreference

Especially the exclusion paths.

Sometimes the most important finding is not what Defender detected.

It is what Defender was told not to look at.

items.content:
RT @VitalikButerin: I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

items.content:
RT @secparam: There’s a risk AI breaks cryptography. Assessing the risk is hard, but assessing folks selling new crypto is not. Don’t fall for it.

There’s no particular reason to think newer math (hash-based crypto, lattices, even QKD) is safer. If you’re worried, you want defense in depth.

Things that make sense: for cryptocurrency, keep cold storage funds in a fresh, unused address. Since addresses, for most systems, are usually  the hash of an ECDSA key, you’d need to break both a hash function and ECDSA.

For encryption, use a hybrid scheme.

What you shouldn’t do: switch to crypto that’s new in the past 10 years because someone tells you it’s more secure.

Many of the folks now saying AI will break crypto were, 5 days ago, saying quantum will break crypto. And ironically, one of the bigger AI crypto breaks was of a post-quantum scheme.
